title: Technology competence: Delegation preserves professional responsibility
desc: Extends competence, supervision and confidentiality duties to technology and outsourcing through proportionate preparation and safeguards.

kps.k: Technology and outsourcing change how lawyers work, not the underlying requirement for competent, ethical representation.
kps.d: The ABA materials locate technological awareness and outsourced work within existing professional duties. Resolution 105A’s report treats explicit technology language as clarification rather than a new obligation; Resolution 105C’s report places outside-lawyer guidance under competence rather than allocation of authority. These materials offer normative standards and ethics reasoning, not empirical evidence of AI effectiveness. The Model Rules and commentary also remain distinct from jurisdictions’ adopted rules.

qs.q: The proposed amendment, which appears in a Comment, does not impose any new obligations on lawyers.

qs.q: The Commission considered other locations for the new commentary, including Model Rule 1.2 (Scope of Representation and Allocation of Authority Between Client and Lawyer), but concluded that the primary ethical consideration when retaining nonfirm lawyers is the competence of those nonfirm lawyers and that Model Rule 1.1 is therefore the appropriate location for further guidance.
qs.a: ABA Commission on Ethics 20/20, Resolution 105C and Report: Outsourcing · Regulators & courts · 2012

kps.k: Competence requires informed use of relevant technology and preparation proportionate to the matter.
kps.d: Model Rule 1.1’s comments connect competence to technology’s benefits and risks, continuing education, factual and legal inquiry, and adequate preparation. They allow lawyers to gain competence through study or association rather than prior experience alone. Rule 1.2’s comments qualify limited-scope arrangements: scope affects the work required, but cannot excuse advice too thin to support client reliance. These general standards do not themselves specify AI verification procedures or require adoption of a particular tool.

qs.q: ### Maintaining Competence  [8] To maintain the requisite knowledge and skill, a lawyer should keep abreast of changes in the law and its practice, including the benefits and risks associated with relevant technology, engage in continuing study and education and comply with all continuing legal education requirements to which the lawyer is subject.
qs.a: ABA Model Rule 1.1: Competence, with Official Comments · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: Although an agreement for a limited representation does not exempt a lawyer from the duty to provide competent representation, the limitation is a factor to be considered when determining the legal knowledge, skill, thoroughness and preparation reasonably necessary for the representation.
qs.a: ABA Model Rule 1.2: Scope of Representation and Allocation of Authority, with Official Comments · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Outsourcing requires differentiated selection, direction and monitoring—not a blanket transfer of responsibility.
kps.d: For outside lawyers, Model Rule 1.1 recommends ordinarily obtaining informed client consent and requires a reasonable belief that their services will contribute to competent, ethical representation. For outside nonlawyers, the guidance calls for reasonable efforts and suitable directions, calibrated to provider qualifications, assigned services, information protections and jurisdictional conditions. Rule 5.3 assigns preventive duties to managers and supervisors and responsibility for specified misconduct they order, knowingly ratify, or knowingly fail to remedy when consequences remain avoidable or mitigable; it does not impose automatic responsibility for every provider error.

qs.q: ### Retaining or Contracting With Other Lawyers  [6] Before a lawyer retains or contracts with other lawyers outside the lawyer’s own firm to provide or assist in the provision of legal services to a client, the lawyer should ordinarily obtain informed consent from the client and must reasonably believe that the other lawyers’ services will contribute to the competent and ethical representation of the client.
qs.a: ABA Model Rule 1.1: Competence, with Official Comments · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: including the education, experience and reputation of the nonlawyer; the nature of the services involved; the terms of any arrangements concerning the protection of client information; and the legal and ethical environments of the jurisdictions in which the services will be performed, particularly with regard to confidentiality.
qs.a: ABA Model Rule 5.3: Responsibilities Regarding Nonlawyer Assistance, with Official Comments · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Confidentiality demands reasonable safeguards, not a guarantee against every breach.
kps.d: Revised Resolution 105A distinguishes permission to disclose client information from the duty to prevent inadvertent disclosure or unauthorized access. Consent, implied authorization and specified exceptions constrain disclosure; reasonable preventive efforts govern safeguarding. The commentary states that a breach alone does not violate paragraph 1.6(c) when the lawyer made reasonable efforts. In practice, provider and technology decisions call for attention to information sensitivity, disclosure risk and protective arrangements, rather than either unquestioning reliance or an absolute zero-risk standard.

kps.k: Client involvement and agreed responsibility support delegation but cannot override professional or legal limits.
kps.d: The guidance recommends clarifying roles across firms and agreeing who monitors a client-selected nonlawyer provider, while preserving additional obligations in tribunal proceedings. Resolution 105A frames responsiveness as medium-neutral and requires explanations sufficient for informed decisions. Outsourcing remains subject to unauthorized-practice restrictions, and Rule 1.2 distinguishes permissible legal analysis from knowing assistance with crime or fraud. The supplied KBA E-457 excerpt adds communication and reasonable-fee standards, but does not establish an AI-specific disclosure or pricing rule.

kps.k: The unresolved issue is how to translate broad duties into concrete AI compliance standards.
kps.d: The soft-law article proposes practical guidance that could specify actions sufficient to meet existing obligations. It cites commentary that lawyers need technical as well as legal skills and may consult experts without delegating their professional duties or blindly accepting black-box results. The supplied materials show no direct disagreement over the underlying duties; the open question concerns their operational specificity. Soft law appears here as a proposed bridge, not a demonstrated effective or enforceable regime, and the excerpts do not settle particular AI oversight procedures.

vlens.an: The academia-and-research source accepts the proposition that using technology or technical experts does not displace lawyers’ duties of competence, supervision and professional responsibility. It materially extends the proposition by proposing soft law as a practical bridge between broad professional obligations and concrete compliance actions. Its reasoning is normative: lawyers increasingly require technical as well as legal competence, must not rely uncritically on black-box outputs, and may obtain expert assistance without transferring their own duties. The principal internal qualification is evidentiary and institutional: soft law is presented as a possible means of operationalising existing obligations, not as an empirically validated, enforceable or fully specified AI-oversight regime. Because the curated evidence contains one academic source, it does not establish a broader consensus or permit meaningful comparison across academic viewpoints.

vlens.an: The selected regulators, courts and professional-body materials consistently support the proposition that adopting technology, outsourcing work or limiting a representation changes the means and context of legal service delivery but does not displace the lawyer’s underlying professional responsibility. Their common reasoning is normative rather than empirical: existing duties of competence, confidentiality, communication and supervision apply through context-sensitive standards such as reasonable preparation, informed client involvement, provider assessment, appropriate direction and monitoring, and reasonable information safeguards. Internal variation concerns which duty and relationship receives emphasis. The technology materials treat awareness of relevant technology’s benefits and risks as part of existing competence; the outsourcing materials distinguish outside lawyers from nonlawyer providers and specify different selection, consent and oversight considerations; the confidentiality guidance requires reasonable preventive efforts rather than guaranteeing that no breach will occur; and the limited-scope, client-communication and fee materials show that agreed scope, delegation and technological change remain constrained by competence, informed decision-making and other legal or ethical limits. Some excerpts do not address AI-specific verification, disclosure or pricing procedures, so they support the governing principle without resolving how broad duties should be operationalised for particular AI systems. This conclusion describes only the curated sources supplied and should not be read as representing every regulator, court or professional body.

elens.an: The pre-2015 materials support the proposition that technology use and outsourcing alter the means of legal practice without displacing lawyers’ underlying professional responsibilities. Across these curated ABA Commission materials, the common rationale is that technological awareness belongs within existing competence duties, while delegation to outside lawyers or nonlawyer providers requires context-sensitive selection, direction, client communication, monitoring and confidentiality safeguards. The standards are generally framed in terms of reasonable efforts rather than absolute prevention of error or breach. Material variation lies mainly in emphasis: the technology materials focus on competence, medium-neutral client communication and confidentiality; the outsourcing materials develop informed consent, allocation of responsibility, supervision and unauthorized-practice constraints. The reports explain why these are clarifications of existing duties, whereas the resolutions provide proposed rule and comment language. These closely related normative sources do not provide empirical evidence about technology or AI performance, nor do they specify concrete AI verification procedures; that operational question remains beyond their scope.

qs.q: Comment [6] already encompasses an obligation to remain aware of changes in technology that affect law practice, but the Commission concluded that making this explicit, by addition of the phrase “including the benefits and risks associated with relevant technology,” would offer greater clarity in this area and emphasize the importance of technology to modern law practice.
qs.a: ABA Commission on Ethics 20/20, Resolution 105A and Report: Technology and Confidentiality · Regulators & courts · 2012

elens.an: The 2015–2022 source accepts the proposition’s core: technology use and reliance on technical experts remain governed by lawyers’ existing duties of competence and supervision, and professional responsibility cannot simply be transferred to an expert or a black-box system. It materially extends the proposition by proposing soft law as a practical bridge between broad professional obligations and concrete compliance actions. The principal variation is therefore not disagreement about retained responsibility, but the degree of operational specificity needed. The source argues for more actionable guidance while stopping short of establishing particular AI verification procedures, enforceable standards, or empirical evidence that soft law is effective. Because this is a single source from a curated corpus, its position should not be treated as representative of the period as a whole.

elens.an: The 2023–2024 source supports the proposition’s core claim that generative AI changes the means of legal work without displacing lawyers’ existing professional responsibilities. KBA E-457 grounds AI-related practice in established duties to communicate sufficiently for informed client decisions and to charge reasonable fees. Its support is narrower than the full cluster synthesis: the supplied excerpt does not develop concrete standards for AI competence, delegation, supervision, confidentiality safeguards, or verification. Internal variation therefore concerns which continuing duties are addressed—client communication and fees—rather than disagreement with the proposition. Because this is a curated source, its position should not be treated as representative of all authorities or commentary from the period.

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources support the proposition that technology, outsourcing and limited-scope delivery alter how competence and oversight are applied without transferring or eliminating the lawyer’s professional responsibility. Their common basis is normative rather than empirical: the ABA Model Rules and official comments require context-sensitive preparation, informed consideration of technology’s benefits and risks, and reasonable assurance that outside assistance is compatible with professional obligations. There is material variation in emphasis. Rule 1.1 addresses continuing technological competence and the selection of outside lawyers; Rule 5.3 focuses on directing and monitoring outside nonlawyers, including client-agreed allocations of monitoring responsibility; and Rule 1.2 establishes that limited representation remains subject to competence and other legal and ethical limits, including the prohibition on knowingly assisting crime or fraud. These sources do not materially extend the synthesis into concrete AI verification or compliance procedures, nor do they provide evidence about AI effectiveness. They therefore support, rather than build materially beyond, the cluster’s principal proposition.
